title: The Art of Decision-Making
excerpt: Your life choices aren’t just about what you want to do, Joshua Rothman writes—they’re about who you want to be.
content_html:
Your life choices aren’t just about what you want to do; they’re about who you want to be.

January 14, 2019

In July of 1838, Charles Darwin was twenty-nine years old and single. Two years earlier, he had returned from his voyage aboard H.M.S. Beagle with the observations that would eventually form the basis of “On the Origin of Species.” In the meantime, he faced a more pressing analytical problem. Darwin was considering proposing to his cousin Emma Wedgwood, but he worried that marriage and children might impede his scientific career. To figure out what to do, he made two lists. “Loss of time,” he wrote on the first. “Perhaps quarreling. . . . Cannot read in the evenings. . . . Anxiety and responsibility. Perhaps my wife won’t like London; then the sentence is banishment and degradation into indolent, idle fool.” On the second, he wrote, “Children (if it Please God). Constant companion (and friend in old age). . . . Home, & someone to take care of house.” He noted that it was “intolerable to think of spending one’s whole life, like a neuter bee, working, working. . . . Only picture to yourself a nice soft wife on a sofa with good fire and books and music perhaps.”

Beneath his lists, Darwin scrawled, “Marry, Marry, Marry QED.” And yet, Steven Johnson writes, in “Farsighted: How We Make the Decisions That Matter the Most,” “we have no evidence of how he actually weighed these competing arguments against each other.” Johnson, the author of “How We Got to Now” and other popular works of intellectual history, can’t help but notice the mediocrity of Darwin’s decision-making process. He points out that Benjamin Franklin used a more advanced pro-and-con technique: in what Franklin called “Prudential Algebra,” a numerical weight is assigned to each listed item, and counterbalancing items are then eliminated. (“If I find a Reason pro equal to some two Reasons con, I strike out the three . . . and thus proceeding I find at length where the Ballance lies,” Franklin explained to a friend.) Even this approach, Johnson writes, is slapdash and dependent upon intuition. “The craft of making farsighted choices—decisions that require long periods of deliberation, decisions whose consequences might last for years,” he concludes, “is a strangely under-appreciated skill.”

We say that we “decide” to get married, to have children, to live in particular cities or embark on particular careers, and in a sense this is true. But how do we actually make those choices? One of the paradoxes of life is that our big decisions are often less calculated than our small ones are. We agonize over what to stream on Netflix, then let TV shows persuade us to move to New York; buying a new laptop may involve weeks of Internet research, but the deliberations behind a life-changing breakup could consist of a few bottles of wine. We’re hardly more advanced than the ancient Persians, who, Herodotus says, made big decisions by discussing them twice: once while drunk, once while sober.

Johnson hopes to reform us. He examines a number of complex decisions with far-reaching consequences—such as the choice, made by President Barack Obama and his advisers, to green-light the raid on Osama bin Laden’s presumed compound, in Abbottabad, Pakistan—and then shows how the people in charge drew upon insights from “decision science,” a research field at the intersection of behavioral economics, psychology, and management. He thinks that we should apply such techniques to our own lives.

I’ve never had to decide whether to launch a covert raid on a suspected terrorist compound, but I’ve made my share of big decisions. This past summer, my wife and I had a baby boy. His existence suggests that, at some point, I decided to become a father. Did I, though? I never practiced any prudential algebra; rather than drawing up lists of pros and cons and concluding, on balance, that having kids was a good idea, I gradually and unintentionally transitioned from not particularly wanting children to wanting them, and from wanting them to joining my wife in having them. If I made a decision, it wasn’t a very decisive one. In “War and Peace,” Tolstoy writes that, while an armchair general may imagine himself “analyzing some campaign on a map” and then issuing orders, a real general never finds himself at “the beginning of some event”; instead, he is perpetually situated in the middle of a series of events, each a link in an endless chain of causation. “Can it be that I allowed Napoleon to get as far as Moscow?” Tolstoy’s General Kutuzov wonders. “When was it decided? Was it yesterday, when I sent Platov the order to retreat, or was it the evening before, when I dozed off and told Bennigsen to give the orders? Or still earlier?” Unlike the capture of Moscow by Napoleon, the birth of my son was a joyous occasion. Still, like Kutuzov, I’m at a loss to explain it: it’s a momentous choice, but I can’t pinpoint the making of it in space or time.

For Tolstoy, the tendency of big decisions to make themselves was one of the great mysteries of existence. It suggested that the stories we tell about our lives are inadequate to their real complexity. Johnson means to offer a way out of the Tolstoyan conundrum. He wants to make us writers, rather than readers, of our own stories. Doing so requires engaging with one of life’s fundamental questions: Are we in charge of the ways we change?

Ideally, we’d be omniscient and clearheaded. In reality, we make decisions in imperfect conditions that prevent us from thinking things through. This, Johnson explains, is the problem of “bounded rationality.” Choices are constrained by earlier choices; facts go undiscovered, ignored, or misunderstood; decision-makers are compromised by groupthink and by their own fallible minds. The most complex decisions harbor “conflicting objectives” and “undiscovered options,” requiring us to predict future possibilities that can be grasped, confusingly, only at “varied levels of uncertainty.” (The likelihood of marital quarrelling must somehow be compared with that of producing a scientific masterwork.) And life’s truly consequential choices, Johnson says, “can’t be understood on a single scale.” Suppose you’re offered two jobs: one at Partners in Health, which brings medical care to the world’s neediest people, and the other at Goldman Sachs. You must consider which option would be most appealing today, later this year, and decades from now; which would be preferable emotionally, financially, and morally; and which is better for you, your family, and society. From this multidimensional matrix, a decision must emerge.

Professional deciders, Johnson reports, use decision processes to navigate this complexity. Many of the best processes unfold in stages—a divergence stage might precede a convergence stage—and are undertaken by groups. (Darwin might have divided his friends into two opposing teams, in the divergence stage, and then held a debate between them.) The decision might be turned into an iterative adventure. In a series of meetings known as a “design charrette”—the concept is borrowed from the field of product design—a large problem is divided into subproblems, each of which is assigned to a group; the groups then present their work to the whole team, receive feedback, regroup, and revise, in a cycle that loops until a decision has been made. (For architects in nineteenth-century Paris, working en charrette meant revising until the very last minute, even in the cart on the way to deliver a design to a panel of judges.) Charrettes are useful not just because they break up the work but because they force groups with different priorities and sensibilities—coders and designers, architects and real-estate developers—to interact, broadening the range of available viewpoints.

At firms like Royal Dutch Shell, where growth requires investing in expensive ventures, such as ports, wells, and pipelines, deciders use “scenario planning” to imagine how such investments might play out. (A scenario-planning starter kit, Johnson writes, contains three possible futures: “You build one model where things get better, one where they get worse, and one where they get weird.”) Military planners use immersive war games, carried out in the field or around a table, to bring more of the “decision map” into view. In such games, our enemies discover possibilities that we can’t foresee, ameliorating the poverty of our individual imaginations. And since the games can be played over and over, they allow decision-makers to “rewind the tape,” exploring many branches of the “decision tree.”

It would be strange to stage a war game about a prospective marriage. Still, Johnson writes, decision science has lessons for us as individuals. Late in “Farsighted,” he recounts his own use of decision-scientific strategies to persuade his wife to move, with their two children, from New York City to the Bay Area. Johnson starts with intuitions—redwoods are beautiful; the tech scene is cool—but quickly moves beyond them. He conducts a “full-spectrum analysis,” arriving at various conclusions about what moving might mean financially, psychologically (will moving to a new city make him feel younger?), and existentially (will he want to have been “the kind of person who lived in one place for most of his adult life”?). Johnson summarizes his findings in a PowerPoint deck, then shows it to his wife, who raises objections that he hasn’t foreseen (all her friends live in Brooklyn). Eventually, they make a contract. They’ll move, but if after two years she wants to return to New York they’ll do so, “no questions asked”—a rewind.

Seven years later, they’re happy with a bicoastal existence. Would Johnson have benefitted from “conducting a multidisciplinary charrette” to explore his family’s move? Probably not. Still, he writes, the principles of decision science—“seeking out diverse perspectives on the choice, challenging your assumptions, making an explicit effort to map the variables”—constituted “a step up” from the pro-and-con lists that Franklin and Darwin would have made. Looking back on his decision, Johnson can at least feel confident that he made one.

Johnson’s book is part of a long tradition. For centuries, philosophers have tried to understand how we make decisions and, by extension, what makes any given decision sound or unsound, rational or irrational. “Decision theory,” the destination on which they’ve converged, has tended to hold that sound decisions flow from values. Faced with a choice—should we major in economics or in art history?—we first ask ourselves what we value, then seek to maximize that value.

From this perspective, a decision is essentially a value-maximizing equation. If you’re going out and can’t decide whether to take an umbrella, you could come to a decision by following a formula that assigns weights to the probability of rain, the pleasure you’ll feel in strolling unencumbered, and the displeasure you’ll feel if you get wet. Most decisions are more complex than this, but the promise of decision theory is that there’s a formula for everything, from launching a raid in Abbottabad to digging an oil well in the North Sea. Plug in your values, and the right choice pops out.

In recent decades, some philosophers have grown dissatisfied with decision theory. They point out that it becomes less useful when we’re unsure what we care about, or when we anticipate that what we care about might shift. In a 2006 article called “Big Decisions: Opting, Converting, Drifting,” the late Israeli philosopher Edna Ullmann-Margalit asked us to imagine being one of “the early socialist Zionist pioneers” who, at the turn of the twentieth century, dreamed of moving from Europe to Palestine and becoming “the New Jews of their ideals.” Such a change, she observed, “alters one’s life project and inner core”; one might speak of an “Old Person” who existed beforehand, browsing bookshops in Budapest, and a “New Person” who exists afterward, working a field in the desert. The point of such a move isn’t to maximize one’s values. It’s to reconfigure them, rewriting the equations by which one is currently living one’s life.

Ullmann-Margalit doubted that such transformative choices could be evaluated as sound or unsound, rational or irrational. She tells the story of a man who “hesitated to have children because he did not want to become the ‘boring type’ ” that parents tend to become. “Finally, he did decide to have a child and, with time, he did adopt the boring characteristics of his parent friends—but he was happy!” Whose values were maximized—Old Person’s or New Person’s? Because no value-maximizing formula could capture such a choice, Ullmann-Margalit suggested that, rather than describing this man as having “decided” to have children, we say that he “opted” to have them—“opting” (in her usage) being what we do when we shift our values instead of maximizing them.

The nature of “opting situations,” she thought, explains why people “are in fact more casual and cavalier in the way they handle their big decisions than in the way they handle their ordinary decisions.” Yet it’s our unexplored options that haunt us. A decision-maker who buys a Subaru doesn’t dwell on the Toyota that might have been: the Toyota doesn’t represent a version of herself with different values. An opter, however, broods over “the person one did not marry, the country one did not emigrate to, the career one did not pursue,” seeing, in the “shadow presence” implied by the rejected option, “a yardstick” by which she might evaluate “the worth, success or meaning” of her actual life.

One might hope that a little research could bridge the divide between Old Person and New Person. In a 2013 paper titled “What You Can’t Expect When You’re Expecting,” L. A. Paul, a philosopher at Yale, writes, “Perhaps you think that you can know what it’s like to have a child, even though you’ve never had one, because you can read or listen to the testimony of what it was like for others. You are wrong.” Paul cites the philosopher David Lewis, who proposed what might be called the Vegemite Principle: if you’ve never tasted Vegemite, a mysterious and beloved Australian “food spread” made from brewer’s yeast, then neither a description of what it’s like (black, gooey, vegetal) nor experience with other spreads (peanut butter, marmalade, Nutella) will suffice to tell you whether you’d like it. Similarly, Paul argues, “being around other people’s children isn’t enough to learn about what it will be like in your own case.” She explains:

Babysitting for other children, having nieces and nephews or much younger siblings—all of these can be wonderful (or horrible) experiences, but they are different in kind from having a child of your very own, perhaps roughly analogous to the way an original artwork has aesthetic value partly because of its origins. . . . Experience with other people’s children might teach you about what it is like to hold a baby, to change diapers or hold a bottle, but not what it is like to create, carry, give birth to and raise a child of your very own.

Before having children, you may enjoy clubbing, skydiving, and LSD; you might find fulfillment in careerism, travel, cooking, or CrossFit; you may simply relish your freedom to do what you want. Having children will deprive you of these joys. And yet, as a parent, you may not miss them. You may actually prefer changing diapers, wrangling onesies, and watching “Frozen.” These activities may sound like torture to the childless version of yourself, but the parental version may find them illuminated by love, and so redeemed. You may end up becoming a different person—a parent. The problem is that you can’t really know, in advance, what “being a parent” is like. For Paul, there’s something thrilling about this quandary. Why should today’s values determine tomorrow’s? In her 2014 book, “Transformative Experience,” she suggests that living “authentically” requires occasionally leaving your old self behind “to create and discover a new self.” Part of being alive is awaiting the “revelation” of “who you’ll become.”

In the months before our son was born, our sense of our ignorance mounted. “We don’t know what we’re waiting for,” my wife said. We knew in advance when he would be born—an ultrasound had revealed that he was unusually big, and a C-section had been scheduled—but the morning of his arrival unfolded with a strange familiarity. I had coffee, toasted an English muffin, and read the news; I packed clothes for the hospital into the bag that I take to work every day. At eleven, my wife and I got into the car. Her mother and a family friend drove us. At the front entrance, we hugged them goodbye.

“Good luck!” my mother-in-law said. “Your lives are about to change forever!”

“Thanks,” I said. “Where are you guys going?”

“Costco,” she said.

We walked inside. Upstairs, in a curtained-off nook, my wife settled into a hospital bed. For about an hour, we made small talk with the nurses, who guessed at the baby’s weight, and with the surgeon, who happened to be a college classmate of ours. (“Heyyyyy! ” she said when she arrived.) Occasionally we were left to ourselves. We held hands and looked at each other.

Eventually, an aide helped my wife into a wheelchair. Flanked by two nurses and wearing oversized scrubs, I pushed her down a long hallway toward the operating room. Inside, the doctors were listening to “Stairway to Heaven” on the radio. In the midst of it all, I admired Jimmy Page’s guitar solo. Afterward, I sat in the same hallway holding our baby. I had wondered if, meeting him for the first time, I would feel transformed. I felt like the same old me. And yet none of the words I knew matched the experience I was having. With my hands, I felt him breathing. Quiet and still, warm and awake, he watched me with dark-blue eyes—an actual new person.

Agnes Callard, a philosopher at the University of Chicago, is skeptical about the idea of sudden transformation. She’s also convinced that, no matter how it looks or feels, we choose how we change. In her often moving, quietly profound book “Aspiration: The Agency of Becoming,” she writes that “becoming a parent is neither something that just happens to you nor something you decide to have happen to you.” Instead, Callard maintains, we “aspire” to self-transformation by trying on the values that we hope one day to possess, just as we might strike a pose in the mirror before heading out on a date. Of the man in Ullmann-Margalit’s article who feared becoming a boring dad, Callard writes, “By the time he says, ‘Let’s go for it,’ he is actively trying to appreciate the values distinctive of parenthood.” In place of a moment of decision, Callard sees a more gradual process: “Old Person aspires to become New Person.”

Suppose that you sign up for a classical-music-appreciation class, in which your first assignment is to listen to a symphony. You put on headphones, press Play—and fall asleep. The problem is that you don’t actually want to listen to classical music; you just want to want to. Aspiring, Callard thinks, is a common human activity: there are aspiring wine lovers, art appreciators, sports fans, fashionistas, d.j.s, executives, alpinists, do-gooders, parents, and religious believers, all hatching plans to value new things. Many ordinary decisions, moreover—such as choosing between Goldman Sachs and Partners in Health—also touch on the question of who we aspire to become.

Callard distinguishes between aspiration and ambition. Some of the people taking the music-appreciation class are ambitious; they enrolled not because they aspire to love classical music but because the class is an easy A. From the first day, they know what they value: their grades. (“Turning ambition into aspiration is one of the job descriptions of any teacher,” Callard notes.) The ambitious students find it easy to explain why they’re taking the class. But the aspirants must grow comfortable with a certain quantity of awkward pretense. If someone were to ask you why you enrolled, you would be overreaching if you said that you were moved by the profound beauty of classical music. The truth, which is harder to communicate, is that you have some vague sense of its value, which you hope that some future version of yourself might properly grasp.

Until aspirants can fully explain their motivations, they often understate their aims. An aspiring painter will say that she finds painting relaxing rather than try to explain what she hopes to express through her art. An aspiration, Callard concludes, has two faces: a near face, which represents it “as lesser than it is,” and a distant one, which an aspirant is reluctant to describe, because it “ennobles her current activity beyond its rightful status.”

Being a well-meaning phony is key to our self-transformations. “Consider what kind of thinking motivates a good student to force herself to listen to a symphony when she feels herself dozing off,” Callard writes:

She reminds herself that her grade and the teacher’s opinion of her depend on the essay she will write about this piece; or she promises herself a chocolate treat when she gets to the end; or she’s in a glass-walled listening room of the library, conscious of other students’ eyes on her; or perhaps she conjures up a romanticized image of her future, musical self, such as that of entering the warm light of a concert hall on a snowy evening.

These are “bad” reasons for listening to classical music, Callard says, but “ ‘bad’ reasons are how she moves herself forward, all the while seeing them as bad, which is to say, as placeholders for the ‘real’ reason.”

When we’re aspiring, inarticulateness isn’t a sign of unreasonableness or incapacity. In fact, the opposite may be true. “Everyone goes to college ‘to become educated,’ ” Callard observes, “but until I am educated I do not really know what an education is or why it is important.” If we couldn’t aspire to changes that we struggle to describe, we’d be trapped within the ideas that we already have. Our inability to explain our reasons is a measure of how far we wish to travel. It’s only after an aspirant has reached her destination, Callard writes, that “she will say, ‘This was why.’ ”

Because aspirations take a long time to come to fruition, they’re always at risk of interruption. Ullmann-Margalit’s 2006 paper makes mention of someone who opts “to leave the corporate world in order to become an artist.” Callard sees that sort of move as the result of an aspiration—a process that starts small, perhaps with a random stroll through an art museum, and culminates, years later, after one opens a pottery studio. The trouble is that some values preclude others. An aspiring artist must reject the corporate virtues to which he once aspired and embrace creative ones in their place. If a family illness forces him to abandon his artistic plans, he may end up adrift—disenchanted with corporate life, but unable to grasp the real satisfactions of an artistic existence. To aspire, Callard writes, is to judge one’s present-day self by the standards of a future self who doesn’t yet exist. But that can leave us like a spider plant putting down roots in the air, hoping for soil that may never arrive.

Callard revisits Paul’s “What You Can’t Expect When You’re Expecting.” In that paper, Paul explored a strange consequence of the Vegemite Principle: if there’s no rational way to decide to have a child—because you can’t know what you’ve never experienced—then there’s also no rational reason for being disappointed about not having one. (Such disappointment isn’t “wrong, or blameworthy, or subjectively unreasonable,” Paul notes—just nonrational.) Callard disagrees. She sees infertility as a form of interrupted aspiration. An aspiring mother who can’t have children is rational in feeling sad, she writes, and “this is so even if—indeed, it is true in part because—she cannot quite see what she would be missing.”

Before we had our son, I began exploring the “near face” of being a parent. I noticed how cute babies and children could be and pictured our spare room as a nursery; I envisaged my wife and I taking our child to the beach near our house (my version of “entering the warm light of a concert hall on a snowy evening”). I knew that these imaginings weren’t the real facts about having children—clearly, there was more to having kids than cuteness. All the same, I had no way of grasping the “distant face” of fatherhood. It was something I aspired to know.

As it turned out, my wife and I had trouble having children. It took us five years to navigate the infertility maze. For much of that time, we lived with what Callard describes as the “distinctive kind of sadness appropriate to losing something you were only starting to try to get to know.” This sadness, Callard points out, has a complement in the disappointment one might feel after “having to abandon one’s educational aspirations for motherhood”: “The aspiring college student who must give up those dreams to raise a child is liable to feel that she was counting on the college experience to make her life meaningful.” Callard quotes from “Barren in the Promised Land,” a book about infertility by the historian Elaine Tyler May. “The grief—the loss,” a woman tells May. “I spent six years of my life trying to be a mom, and it was beyond my control. For a while I couldn’t look ahead. I thought, how do I define myself if I don’t do this? What am I if not a parent?” It might be easier if our biggest transformations were instantaneous, because then we wouldn’t need to live in states of aspiration. Certain of who we were, we’d never get stuck between selves.

I read “Aspiration” last spring, before my son was born, and I talked about it often with my wife. We were especially struck by Callard’s argument that parenthood is intrinsically aspirational. Parents look forward to a loving relationship with a specific person. And yet that person doesn’t pop into existence fully formed; he emerges, in all his specificity, over many years. For this reason, it makes little sense to be an “ambitious parent”—someone who plans, in advance, what he will love about his child. It’s better to “enter parenthood for the most inchoate of reasons,” Callard concludes, since that “puts our children in a position to fill out what parenthood means for us”; in turn, parental love must “be capable of molding itself to the personality that is, itself, coming to take a determinate shape.”

For the most part, Callard’s book is a systematic overview, situated outside the moment. Still, she writes, for aspirants “what happens in the meanwhile is also life.” Now that our son is here, we live entirely in the meanwhile. We don’t want the present, or its mystery, to end. Each day is absorbing and endlessly significant. Recently, I watched my father’s face as he watched my son’s. Later, we listened as my son learned a new kind of laugh. Each time he looks at us, he sees us more in his own way. Like pages that turn themselves, the meaningful instants follow one another too soon. It’s hard to think of them as stepping stones on the way to anywhere else. ♦

In a series of meetings known as a “design charrette”—the concept is borrowed from the field of product design—a large problem is divided into subproblems, each of which is assigned to a group; the groups then present their work to the whole team, receive feedback, regroup, and revise, in a cycle that loops until a decision has been made. (For architects in nineteenth-century Paris, working en charrette meant revising until the very last minute, even in the cart on the way to deliver a design to a panel of judges.) Charrettes are useful not just because they break up the work but because they force groups with different priorities and sensibilities—coders and designers, architects and real-estate developers—to interact, broadening the range of available viewpoints.At firms like Royal Dutch Shell, where growth requires investing in expensive ventures, such as ports, wells, and pipelines, deciders use “scenario planning” to imagine how such investments might play out. (A scenario-planning starter kit, Johnson writes, contains three possible futures: “You build one model where things get better, one where they get worse, and one where they get weird.”) Military planners use immersive war games, carried out in the field or around a table, to bring more of the “decision map” into view. In such games, our enemies discover possibilities that we can’t foresee, ameliorating the poverty of our individual imaginations. And since the games can be played over and over, they allow decision-makers to “rewind the tape,” exploring many branches of the “decision tree.”It would be strange to stage a war game about a prospective marriage. Still, Johnson writes, decision science has lessons for us as individuals. Late in “Farsighted,” he recounts his own use of decision-scientific strategies to persuade his wife to move, with their two children, from New York City to the Bay Area. Johnson starts with intuitions—redwoods are beautiful; the tech scene is cool—but quickly moves beyond them. He conducts a “full-spectrum analysis,” arriving at various conclusions about what moving might mean financially, psychologically (will moving to a new city make him feel younger?), and existentially (will he want to have been “the kind of person who lived in one place for most of his adult life”?). Johnson summarizes his findings in a PowerPoint deck, then shows it to his wife, who raises objections that he hasn’t foreseen (all her friends live in Brooklyn). Eventually, they make a contract. They’ll move, but if after two years she wants to return to New York they’ll do so, “no questions asked”—a rewind.Seven years later, they’re happy with a bicoastal existence. Would Johnson have benefitted from “conducting a multidisciplinary charrette” to explore his family’s move? Probably not. Still, he writes, the principles of decision science—“seeking out diverse perspectives on the choice, challenging your assumptions, making an explicit effort to map the variables”—constituted “a step up” from the pro-and-con lists that Franklin and Darwin would have made. Looking back on his decision, Johnson can at least feel confident that he made one.Johnson’s book is part of a long tradition. For centuries, philosophers have tried to understand how we make decisions and, by extension, what makes any given decision sound or unsound, rational or irrational. “Decision theory,” the destination on which they’ve converged, has tended to hold that sound decisions flow from values. Faced with a choice—should we major in economics or in art history?—we first ask ourselves what we value, then seek to maximize that value.From this perspective, a decision is essentially a value-maximizing equation. If you’re going out and can’t decide whether to take an umbrella, you could come to a decision by following a formula that assigns weights to the probability of rain, the pleasure you’ll feel in strolling unencumbered, and the displeasure you’ll feel if you get wet. Most decisions are more complex than this, but the promise of decision theory is that there’s a formula for everything, from launching a raid in Abbottabad to digging an oil well in the North Sea. Plug in your values, and the right choice pops out.In recent decades, some philosophers have grown dissatisfied with decision theory. They point out that it becomes less useful when we’re unsure what we care about, or when we anticipate that what we care about might shift. In a 2006 article called “Big Decisions: Opting, Converting, Drifting,” the late Israeli philosopher Edna Ullmann-Margalit asked us to imagine being one of “the early socialist Zionist pioneers” who, at the turn of the twentieth century, dreamed of moving from Europe to Palestine and becoming “the New Jews of their ideals.” Such a change, she observed, “alters one’s life project and inner core”; one might speak of an “Old Person” who existed beforehand, browsing bookshops in Budapest, and a “New Person” who exists afterward, working a field in the desert. The point of such a move isn’t to maximize one’s values. It’s to reconfigure them, rewriting the equations by which one is currently living one’s life.Ullmann-Margalit doubted that such transformative choices could be evaluated as sound or unsound, rational or irrational. She tells the story of a man who “hesitated to have children because he did not want to become the ‘boring type’ ” that parents tend to become. “Finally, he did decide to have a child and, with time, he did adopt the boring characteristics of his parent friends—but he was happy!” Whose values were maximized—Old Person’s or New Person’s? Because no value-maximizing formula could capture such a choice, Ullmann-Margalit suggested that, rather than describing this man as having “decided” to have children, we say that he “opted” to have them—“opting” (in her usage) being what we do when we shift our values instead of maximizing them.The nature of “opting situations,” she thought, explains why people “are in fact more casual and cavalier in the way they handle their big decisions than in the way they handle their ordinary decisions.” Yet it’s our unexplored options that haunt us. A decision-maker who buys a Subaru doesn’t dwell on the Toyota that might have been: the Toyota doesn’t represent a version of herself with different values. An opter, however, broods over “the person one did not marry, the country one did not emigrate to, the career one did not pursue,” seeing, in the “shadow presence” implied by the rejected option, “a yardstick” by which she might evaluate “the worth, success or meaning” of her actual life.One might hope that a little research could bridge the divide between Old Person and New Person. In a 2013 paper titled “What You Can’t Expect When You’re Expecting,” L. A. Paul, a philosopher at Yale, writes, “Perhaps you think that you can know what it’s like to have a child, even though you’ve never had one, because you can read or listen to the testimony of what it was like for others. You are wrong.” Paul cites the philosopher David Lewis, who proposed what might be called the Vegemite Principle: if you’ve never tasted Vegemite, a mysterious and beloved Australian “food spread” made from brewer’s yeast, then neither a description of what it’s like (black, gooey, vegetal) nor experience with other spreads (peanut butter, marmalade, Nutella) will suffice to tell you whether you’d like it. Similarly, Paul argues, “being around other people’s children isn’t enough to learn about what it will be like in your own case.” She explains:Babysitting for other children, having nieces and nephews or much younger siblings—all of these can be wonderful (or horrible) experiences, but they are different in kind from having a child of your very own, perhaps roughly analogous to the way an original artwork has aesthetic value partly because of its origins. . . . Experience with other people’s children might teach you about what it is like to hold a baby, to change diapers or hold a bottle, but not what it is like to create, carry, give birth to and raise a child of your very own.Before having children, you may enjoy clubbing, skydiving, and LSD; you might find fulfillment in careerism, travel, cooking, or CrossFit; you may simply relish your freedom to do what you want. Having children will deprive you of these joys. And yet, as a parent, you may not miss them. You may actually prefer changing diapers, wrangling onesies, and watching “Frozen.” These activities may sound like torture to the childless version of yourself, but the parental version may find them illuminated by love, and so redeemed. You may end up becoming a different person—a parent. The problem is that you can’t really know, in advance, what “being a parent” is like. For Paul, there’s something thrilling about this quandary. Why should today’s values determine tomorrow’s? In her 2014 book, “Transformative Experience,” she suggests that living “authentically” requires occasionally leaving your old self behind “to create and discover a new self.” Part of being alive is awaiting the “revelation” of “who you’ll become.”In the months before our son was born, our sense of our ignorance mounted. “We don’t know what we’re waiting for,” my wife said. We knew in advance when he would be born—an ultrasound had revealed that he was unusually big, and a C-section had been scheduled—but the morning of his arrival unfolded with a strange familiarity. I had coffee, toasted an English muffin, and read the news; I packed clothes for the hospital into the bag that I take to work every day. At eleven, my wife and I got into the car. Her mother and a family friend drove us. At the front entrance, we hugged them goodbye.“You’re awfully quiet tonight.”Cartoon by Lars Kenseth“Good luck!” my mother-in-law said. “Your lives are about to change forever!”“Thanks,” I said. “Where are you guys going?”“Costco,” she said.We walked inside. Upstairs, in a curtained-off nook, my wife settled into a hospital bed. For about an hour, we made small talk with the nurses, who guessed at the baby’s weight, and with the surgeon, who happened to be a college classmate of ours. (“Heyyyyy! ” she said when she arrived.) Occasionally we were left to ourselves. We held hands and looked at each other.Eventually, an aide helped my wife into a wheelchair. Flanked by two nurses and wearing oversized scrubs, I pushed her down a long hallway toward the operating room. Inside, the doctors were listening to “Stairway to Heaven” on the radio. In the midst of it all, I admired Jimmy Page’s guitar solo. Afterward, I sat in the same hallway holding our baby. I had wondered if, meeting him for the first time, I would feel transformed. I felt like the same old me. And yet none of the words I knew matched the experience I was having. With my hands, I felt him breathing. Quiet and still, warm and awake, he watched me with dark-blue eyes—an actual new person.Agnes Callard, a philosopher at the University of Chicago, is skeptical about the idea of sudden transformation. She’s also convinced that, no matter how it looks or feels, we choose how we change. In her often moving, quietly profound book “Aspiration: The Agency of Becoming,” she writes that “becoming a parent is neither something that just happens to you nor something you decide to have happen to you.” Instead, Callard maintains, we “aspire” to self-transformation by trying on the values that we hope one day to possess, just as we might strike a pose in the mirror before heading out on a date. Of the man in Ullmann-Margalit’s article who feared becoming a boring dad, Callard writes, “By the time he says, ‘Let’s go for it,’ he is actively trying to appreciate the values distinctive of parenthood.” In place of a moment of decision, Callard sees a more gradual process: “Old Person aspires to become New Person.”Suppose that you sign up for a classical-music-appreciation class, in which your first assignment is to listen to a symphony. You put on headphones, press Play—and fall asleep. The problem is that you don’t actually want to listen to classical music; you just want to want to. Aspiring, Callard thinks, is a common human activity: there are aspiring wine lovers, art appreciators, sports fans, fashionistas, d.j.s, executives, alpinists, do-gooders, parents, and religious believers, all hatching plans to value new things. Many ordinary decisions, moreover—such as choosing between Goldman Sachs and Partners in Health—also touch on the question of who we aspire to become.Callard distinguishes between aspiration and ambition. Some of the people taking the music-appreciation class are ambitious; they enrolled not because they aspire to love classical music but because the class is an easy A. From the first day, they know what they value: their grades. (“Turning ambition into aspiration is one of the job descriptions of any teacher,” Callard notes.) The ambitious students find it easy to explain why they’re taking the class. But the aspirants must grow comfortable with a certain quantity of awkward pretense. If someone were to ask you why you enrolled, you would be overreaching if you said that you were moved by the profound beauty of classical music. The truth, which is harder to communicate, is that you have some vague sense of its value, which you hope that some future version of yourself might properly grasp.Until aspirants can fully explain their motivations, they often understate their aims. An aspiring painter will say that she finds painting relaxing rather than try to explain what she hopes to express through her art. An aspiration, Callard concludes, has two faces: a near face, which represents it “as lesser than it is,” and a distant one, which an aspirant is reluctant to describe, because it “ennobles her current activity beyond its rightful status.”Being a well-meaning phony is key to our self-transformations. “Consider what kind of thinking motivates a good student to force herself to listen to a symphony when she feels herself dozing off,” Callard writes:She reminds herself that her grade and the teacher’s opinion of her depend on the essay she will write about this piece; or she promises herself a chocolate treat when she gets to the end; or she’s in a glass-walled listening room of the library, conscious of other students’ eyes on her; or perhaps she conjures up a romanticized image of her future, musical self, such as that of entering the warm light of a concert hall on a snowy evening.These are “bad” reasons for listening to classical music, Callard says, but “ ‘bad’ reasons are how she moves herself forward, all the while seeing them as bad, which is to say, as placeholders for the ‘real’ reason.”When we’re aspiring, inarticulateness isn’t a sign of unreasonableness or incapacity. In fact, the opposite may be true. “Everyone goes to college ‘to become educated,’ ” Callard observes, “but until I am educated I do not really know what an education is or why it is important.” If we couldn’t aspire to changes that we struggle to describe, we’d be trapped within the ideas that we already have. Our inability to explain our reasons is a measure of how far we wish to travel. It’s only after an aspirant has reached her destination, Callard writes, that “she will say, ‘This was why.’ ”Because aspirations take a long time to come to fruition, they’re always at risk of interruption. Ullmann-Margalit’s 2006 paper makes mention of someone who opts “to leave the corporate world in order to become an artist.” Callard sees that sort of move as the result of an aspiration—a process that starts small, perhaps with a random stroll through an art museum, and culminates, years later, after one opens a pottery studio. The trouble is that some values preclude others. An aspiring artist must reject the corporate virtues to which he once aspired and embrace creative ones in their place. If a family illness forces him to abandon his artistic plans, he may end up adrift—disenchanted with corporate life, but unable to grasp the real satisfactions of an artistic existence. To aspire, Callard writes, is to judge one’s present-day self by the standards of a future self who doesn’t yet exist. But that can leave us like a spider plant putting down roots in the air, hoping for soil that may never arrive.Callard revisits Paul’s “What You Can’t Expect When You’re Expecting.” In that paper, Paul explored a strange consequence of the Vegemite Principle: if there’s no rational way to decide to have a child—because you can’t know what you’ve never experienced—then there’s also no rational reason for being disappointed about not having one. (Such disappointment isn’t “wrong, or blameworthy, or subjectively unreasonable,” Paul notes—just nonrational.) Callard disagrees. She sees infertility as a form of interrupted aspiration. An aspiring mother who can’t have children is rational in feeling sad, she writes, and “this is so even if—indeed, it is true in part because—she cannot quite see what she would be missing.”Before we had our son, I began exploring the “near face” of being a parent. I noticed how cute babies and children could be and pictured our spare room as a nursery; I envisaged my wife and I taking our child to the beach near our house (my version of “entering the warm light of a concert hall on a snowy evening”). I knew that these imaginings weren’t the real facts about having children—clearly, there was more to having kids than cuteness. All the same, I had no way of grasping the “distant face” of fatherhood. It was something I aspired to know.As it turned out, my wife and I had trouble having children. It took us five years to navigate the infertility maze. For much of that time, we lived with what Callard describes as the “distinctive kind of sadness appropriate to losing something you were only starting to try to get to know.” This sadness, Callard points out, has a complement in the disappointment one might feel after “having to abandon one’s educational aspirations for motherhood”: “The aspiring college student who must give up those dreams to raise a child is liable to feel that she was counting on the college experience to make her life meaningful.” Callard quotes from “Barren in the Promised Land,” a book about infertility by the historian Elaine Tyler May. “The grief—the loss,” a woman tells May. “I spent six years of my life trying to be a mom, and it was beyond my control. For a while I couldn’t look ahead. I thought, how do I define myself if I don’t do this? What am I if not a parent?” It might be easier if our biggest transformations were instantaneous, because then we wouldn’t need to live in states of aspiration. Certain of who we were, we’d never get stuck between selves.I read “Aspiration” last spring, before my son was born, and I talked about it often with my wife. We were especially struck by Callard’s argument that parenthood is intrinsically aspirational. Parents look forward to a loving relationship with a specific person. And yet that person doesn’t pop into existence fully formed; he emerges, in all his specificity, over many years. For this reason, it makes little sense to be an “ambitious parent”—someone who plans, in advance, what he will love about his child. It’s better to “enter parenthood for the most inchoate of reasons,” Callard concludes, since that “puts our children in a position to fill out what parenthood means for us”; in turn, parental love must “be capable of molding itself to the personality that is, itself, coming to take a determinate shape.”For the most part, Callard’s book is a systematic overview, situated outside the moment. Still, she writes, for aspirants “what happens in the meanwhile is also life.” Now that our son is here, we live entirely in the meanwhile. We don’t want the present, or its mystery, to end. Each day is absorbing and endlessly significant. Recently, I watched my father’s face as he watched my son’s. Later, we listened as my son learned a new kind of laugh. Each time he looks at us, he sees us more in his own way. Like pages that turn themselves, the meaningful instants follow one another too soon. It’s hard to think of them as stepping stones on the way to anywhere else. ♦Read More

blocks.html_en: In July of 1838, Charles Darwin was twenty-nine years old and single. Two years earlier, he had returned from his voyage aboard H.M.S. Beagle with the observations that would eventually form the basis of “On the Origin of Species.” In the meantime, he faced a more pressing analytical problem. Darwin was considering proposing to his cousin Emma Wedgwood, but he worried that marriage and children might impede his scientific career. To figure out what to do, he made two lists. “Loss of time,” he wrote on the first. “Perhaps quarreling. . . . Cannot read in the evenings. . . . Anxiety and responsibility. Perhaps my wife won’t like London; then the sentence is banishment and degradation into indolent, idle fool.” On the second, he wrote, “Children (if it Please God). Constant companion (and friend in old age). . . . Home, & someone to take care of house.” He noted that it was “intolerable to think of spending one’s whole life, like a neuter bee, working, working. . . . Only picture to yourself a nice soft wife on a sofa with good fire and books and music perhaps.”

blocks.html_en: Beneath his lists, Darwin scrawled, “Marry, Marry, Marry QED.” And yet, Steven Johnson writes, in “Farsighted: How We Make the Decisions That Matter the Most,” “we have no evidence of how he actually weighed these competing arguments against each other.” Johnson, the author of “How We Got to Now” and other popular works of intellectual history, can’t help but notice the mediocrity of Darwin’s decision-making process. He points out that Benjamin Franklin used a more advanced pro-and-con technique: in what Franklin called “Prudential Algebra,” a numerical weight is assigned to each listed item, and counterbalancing items are then eliminated. (“If I find a Reason pro equal to some two Reasons con, I strike out the three . . . and thus proceeding I find at length where the Ballance lies,” Franklin explained to a friend.) Even this approach, Johnson writes, is slapdash and dependent upon intuition. “The craft of making farsighted choices—decisions that require long periods of deliberation, decisions whose consequences might last for years,” he concludes, “is a strangely under-appreciated skill.”

blocks.html_en: We say that we “decide” to get married, to have children, to live in particular cities or embark on particular careers, and in a sense this is true. But how do we actually make those choices? One of the paradoxes of life is that our big decisions are often less calculated than our small ones are. We agonize over what to stream on Netflix, then let TV shows persuade us to move to New York; buying a new laptop may involve weeks of Internet research, but the deliberations behind a life-changing breakup could consist of a few bottles of wine. We’re hardly more advanced than the ancient Persians, who, Herodotus says, made big decisions by discussing them twice: once while drunk, once while sober.

blocks.html_en: Johnson hopes to reform us. He examines a number of complex decisions with far-reaching consequences—such as the choice, made by President Barack Obama and his advisers, to green-light the raid on Osama bin Laden’s presumed compound, in Abbottabad, Pakistan—and then shows how the people in charge drew upon insights from “decision science,” a research field at the intersection of behavioral economics, psychology, and management. He thinks that we should apply such techniques to our own lives.

blocks.html_en: I’ve never had to decide whether to launch a covert raid on a suspected terrorist compound, but I’ve made my share of big decisions. This past summer, my wife and I had a baby boy. His existence suggests that, at some point, I decided to become a father. Did I, though? I never practiced any prudential algebra; rather than drawing up lists of pros and cons and concluding, on balance, that having kids was a good idea, I gradually and unintentionally transitioned from not particularly wanting children to wanting them, and from wanting them to joining my wife in having them. If I made a decision, it wasn’t a very decisive one. In “War and Peace,” Tolstoy writes that, while an armchair general may imagine himself “analyzing some campaign on a map” and then issuing orders, a real general never finds himself at “the beginning of some event”; instead, he is perpetually situated in the middle of a series of events, each a link in an endless chain of causation. “Can it be that I allowed Napoleon to get as far as Moscow?” Tolstoy’s General Kutuzov wonders. “When was it decided? Was it yesterday, when I sent Platov the order to retreat, or was it the evening before, when I dozed off and told Bennigsen to give the orders? Or still earlier?” Unlike the capture of Moscow by Napoleon, the birth of my son was a joyous occasion. Still, like Kutuzov, I’m at a loss to explain it: it’s a momentous choice, but I can’t pinpoint the making of it in space or time.

blocks.html_en: For Tolstoy, the tendency of big decisions to make themselves was one of the great mysteries of existence. It suggested that the stories we tell about our lives are inadequate to their real complexity. Johnson means to offer a way out of the Tolstoyan conundrum. He wants to make us writers, rather than readers, of our own stories. Doing so requires engaging with one of life’s fundamental questions: Are we in charge of the ways we change?

blocks.html_en: Ideally, we’d be omniscient and clearheaded. In reality, we make decisions in imperfect conditions that prevent us from thinking things through. This, Johnson explains, is the problem of “bounded rationality.” Choices are constrained by earlier choices; facts go undiscovered, ignored, or misunderstood; decision-makers are compromised by groupthink and by their own fallible minds. The most complex decisions harbor “conflicting objectives” and “undiscovered options,” requiring us to predict future possibilities that can be grasped, confusingly, only at “varied levels of uncertainty.” (The likelihood of marital quarrelling must somehow be compared with that of producing a scientific masterwork.) And life’s truly consequential choices, Johnson says, “can’t be understood on a single scale.” Suppose you’re offered two jobs: one at Partners in Health, which brings medical care to the world’s neediest people, and the other at Goldman Sachs. You must consider which option would be most appealing today, later this year, and decades from now; which would be preferable emotionally, financially, and morally; and which is better for you, your family, and society. From this multidimensional matrix, a decision must emerge.

blocks.html_en: Professional deciders, Johnson reports, use decision processes to navigate this complexity. Many of the best processes unfold in stages—a divergence stage might precede a convergence stage—and are undertaken by groups. (Darwin might have divided his friends into two opposing teams, in the divergence stage, and then held a debate between them.) The decision might be turned into an iterative adventure. In a series of meetings known as a “design charrette”—the concept is borrowed from the field of product design—a large problem is divided into subproblems, each of which is assigned to a group; the groups then present their work to the whole team, receive feedback, regroup, and revise, in a cycle that loops until a decision has been made. (For architects in nineteenth-century Paris, working en charrette meant revising until the very last minute, even in the cart on the way to deliver a design to a panel of judges.) Charrettes are useful not just because they break up the work but because they force groups with different priorities and sensibilities—coders and designers, architects and real-estate developers—to interact, broadening the range of available viewpoints.

blocks.html_en: At firms like Royal Dutch Shell, where growth requires investing in expensive ventures, such as ports, wells, and pipelines, deciders use “scenario planning” to imagine how such investments might play out. (A scenario-planning starter kit, Johnson writes, contains three possible futures: “You build one model where things get better, one where they get worse, and one where they get weird.”) Military planners use immersive war games, carried out in the field or around a table, to bring more of the “decision map” into view. In such games, our enemies discover possibilities that we can’t foresee, ameliorating the poverty of our individual imaginations. And since the games can be played over and over, they allow decision-makers to “rewind the tape,” exploring many branches of the “decision tree.”

blocks.html_en: It would be strange to stage a war game about a prospective marriage. Still, Johnson writes, decision science has lessons for us as individuals. Late in “Farsighted,” he recounts his own use of decision-scientific strategies to persuade his wife to move, with their two children, from New York City to the Bay Area. Johnson starts with intuitions—redwoods are beautiful; the tech scene is cool—but quickly moves beyond them. He conducts a “full-spectrum analysis,” arriving at various conclusions about what moving might mean financially, psychologically (will moving to a new city make him feel younger?), and existentially (will he want to have been “the kind of person who lived in one place for most of his adult life”?). Johnson summarizes his findings in a PowerPoint deck, then shows it to his wife, who raises objections that he hasn’t foreseen (all her friends live in Brooklyn). Eventually, they make a contract. They’ll move, but if after two years she wants to return to New York they’ll do so, “no questions asked”—a rewind.

blocks.html_en: Johnson’s book is part of a long tradition. For centuries, philosophers have tried to understand how we make decisions and, by extension, what makes any given decision sound or unsound, rational or irrational. “Decision theory,” the destination on which they’ve converged, has tended to hold that sound decisions flow from values. Faced with a choice—should we major in economics or in art history?—we first ask ourselves what we value, then seek to maximize that value.

blocks.html_en: From this perspective, a decision is essentially a value-maximizing equation. If you’re going out and can’t decide whether to take an umbrella, you could come to a decision by following a formula that assigns weights to the probability of rain, the pleasure you’ll feel in strolling unencumbered, and the displeasure you’ll feel if you get wet. Most decisions are more complex than this, but the promise of decision theory is that there’s a formula for everything, from launching a raid in Abbottabad to digging an oil well in the North Sea. Plug in your values, and the right choice pops out.

blocks.html_en: In recent decades, some philosophers have grown dissatisfied with decision theory. They point out that it becomes less useful when we’re unsure what we care about, or when we anticipate that what we care about might shift. In a 2006 article called “Big Decisions: Opting, Converting, Drifting,” the late Israeli philosopher Edna Ullmann-Margalit asked us to imagine being one of “the early socialist Zionist pioneers” who, at the turn of the twentieth century, dreamed of moving from Europe to Palestine and becoming “the New Jews of their ideals.” Such a change, she observed, “alters one’s life project and inner core”; one might speak of an “Old Person” who existed beforehand, browsing bookshops in Budapest, and a “New Person” who exists afterward, working a field in the desert. The point of such a move isn’t to maximize one’s values. It’s to reconfigure them, rewriting the equations by which one is currently living one’s life.

blocks.html_en: Before having children, you may enjoy clubbing, skydiving, and LSD; you might find fulfillment in careerism, travel, cooking, or CrossFit; you may simply relish your freedom to do what you want. Having children will deprive you of these joys. And yet, as a parent, you may not miss them. You may actually prefer changing diapers, wrangling onesies, and watching “Frozen.” These activities may sound like torture to the childless version of yourself, but the parental version may find them illuminated by love, and so redeemed. You may end up becoming a different person—a parent. The problem is that you can’t really know, in advance, what “being a parent” is like. For Paul, there’s something thrilling about this quandary. Why should today’s values determine tomorrow’s? blocks.html_en: Agnes Callard, a philosopher at the University of Chicago, is skeptical about the idea of sudden transformation. She’s also convinced that, no matter how it looks or feels, we choose how we change. In her often moving, quietly profound book “Aspiration: The Agency of Becoming,” she writes that “becoming a parent is neither something that just happens to you nor something you decide to have happen to you.” Instead, Callard maintains, we “aspire” to self-transformation by trying on the values that we hope one day to possess, just as we might strike a pose in the mirror before heading out on a date. Of the man in Ullmann-Margalit’s article who feared becoming a boring dad, Callard writes, “By the time he says, ‘Let’s go for it,’ he is actively trying to appreciate the values distinctive of parenthood.” In place of a moment of decision, Callard sees a more gradual process: “Old Person aspires to become New Person.”

blocks.html_en: Callard distinguishes between aspiration and ambition. Some of the people taking the music-appreciation class are ambitious; they enrolled not because they aspire to love classical music but because the class is an easy A. From the first day, they know what they value: their grades. (“Turning ambition into aspiration is one of the job descriptions of any teacher,” Callard notes.) The ambitious students find it easy to explain why they’re taking the class. But the aspirants must grow comfortable with a certain quantity of awkward pretense. If someone were to ask you why you enrolled, you would be overreaching if you said that you were moved by the profound beauty of classical music. The truth, which is harder to communicate, is that you have some vague sense of its value, which you hope that some future version of yourself might properly grasp.

blocks.html_en: Because aspirations take a long time to come to fruition, they’re always at risk of interruption. Ullmann-Margalit’s 2006 paper makes mention of someone who opts “to leave the corporate world in order to become an artist.” Callard sees that sort of move as the result of an aspiration—a process that starts small, perhaps with a random stroll through an art museum, and culminates, years later, after one opens a pottery studio. The trouble is that some values preclude others. An aspiring artist must reject the corporate virtues to which he once aspired and embrace creative ones in their place. If a family illness forces him to abandon his artistic plans, he may end up adrift—disenchanted with corporate life, but unable to grasp the real satisfactions of an artistic existence. To aspire, Callard writes, is to judge one’s present-day self by the standards of a future self who doesn’t yet exist. But that can leave us like a spider plant putting down roots in the air, hoping for soil that may never arrive.

blocks.html_en: Callard revisits Paul’s “What You Can’t Expect When You’re Expecting.” In that paper, Paul explored a strange consequence of the Vegemite Principle: if there’s no rational way to decide to have a child—because you can’t know what you’ve never experienced—then there’s also no rational reason for being disappointed about not having one. blocks.html_en: As it turned out, my wife and I had trouble having children. It took us five years to navigate the infertility maze. For much of that time, we lived with what Callard describes as the “distinctive kind of sadness appropriate to losing something you were only starting to try to get to know.” This sadness, Callard points out, has a complement in the disappointment one might feel after “having to abandon one’s educational aspirations for motherhood”: “The aspiring college student who must give up those dreams to raise a child is liable to feel that she was counting on the college experience to make her life meaningful.” Callard quotes from “Barren in the Promised Land,” a book about infertility by the historian Elaine Tyler May. “The grief—the loss,” a woman tells May. “I spent six years of my life trying to be a mom, and it was beyond my control. For a while I couldn’t look ahead. I thought, how do I define myself if I don’t do this? What am I if not a parent?” It might be easier if our biggest transformations were instantaneous, because then we wouldn’t need to live in states of aspiration. Certain of who we were, we’d never get stuck between selves.

blocks.html_en: I read “Aspiration” last spring, before my son was born, and I talked about it often with my wife. We were especially struck by Callard’s argument that parenthood is intrinsically aspirational. Parents look forward to a loving relationship with a specific person. And yet that person doesn’t pop into existence fully formed; he emerges, in all his specificity, over many years. For this reason, it makes little sense to be an “ambitious parent”—someone who plans, in advance, what he will love about his child. It’s better to “enter parenthood for the most inchoate of reasons,” Callard concludes, since that “puts our children in a position to fill out what parenthood means for us”; in turn, parental love must “be capable of molding itself to the personality that is, itself, coming to take a determinate shape.”

sentences.zh: 去年春天，在我儿子出生之前，我读了《愿望》，我经常和我的妻子谈论它。

sentences.en: We were especially struck by Callard’s argument that parenthood is intrinsically aspirational.
sentences.zh: 卡拉德的论点尤其令我们震惊，他认为为人父母本质上是一种渴望。

sentences.en: Parents look forward to a loving relationship with a specific person.
sentences.zh: 父母期待与特定的人建立爱的关系。

sentences.en: And yet that person doesn’t pop into existence fully formed; he emerges, in all his specificity, over many years.
sentences.zh: 然而，这个人并没有完全成形；他还没有完全成型。他的独特性历经了许多年才得以显现。

sentences.en: For this reason, it makes little sense to be an “ambitious parent”—someone who plans, in advance, what he will love about his child.
sentences.zh: 出于这个原因，成为一个“雄心勃勃的父母”——一个提前计划他会爱孩子什么的人——是没有意义的。

sentences.en: It’s better to “enter parenthood for the most inchoate of reasons,” Callard concludes, since that “puts our children in a position to fill out what parenthood means for us”; in turn, parental love must “be capable of molding itself to the personality that is, itself, coming to take a determinate shape.”
sentences.zh: 卡拉德总结道，最好“出于最不成熟的原因而成为父母”，因为这“让我们的孩子能够了解为人父母对我们意味着什么”；反过来，父母的爱必须“能够将自己塑造成人格，而人格本身就会形成确定的形状”。

blocks.html_en: For the most part, Callard’s book is a systematic overview, situated outside the moment. Still, she writes, for aspirants “what happens in the meanwhile is also life.” Now that our son is here, we live entirely in the meanwhile. We don’t want the present, or its mystery, to end. Each day is absorbing and endlessly significant. Recently, I watched my father’s face as he watched my son’s. Later, we listened as my son learned a new kind of laugh. Each time he looks at us, he sees us more in his own way. Like pages that turn themselves, the meaningful instants follow one another too soon. It’s hard to think of them as stepping stones on the way to anywhere else. ♦

content_html_zh:
你的人生选择不仅仅是你想做什么，而是你想做什么。它们与你想成为的人有关。

2019 年 1 月 14 日

1838 年 7 月，查尔斯·达尔文 (Charles Darwin) 二十九岁，单身。 两年前，他乘坐英国皇家海军 (H.M.S.) 航行归来。 贝格尔的观察结果最终构成了《物种起源》的基础。 与此同时，他面临着更紧迫的分析问题。 达尔文正在考虑向他的表弟艾玛·韦奇伍德求婚，但他担心婚姻和孩子可能会阻碍他的科学事业。 为了弄清楚该怎么做，他列出了两个清单。 “浪费了时间，”他在第一封信中写道。 “可能是吵架了……” 晚上不能读书。 。 。 。 焦虑和责任。 也许我的妻子不喜欢伦敦；也许我的妻子不喜欢伦敦。那么判决就是放逐并贬低为懒惰、游手好闲的傻瓜。” 在第二封信中，他写道：“孩子们（如果上帝愿意的话）。 忠实的伴侣（和晚年的朋友）。 。 。 。 家，还有人照顾家。” 他指出，“一想到自己的一生都像一只中性蜜蜂一样工作、工作，就让人难以忍受……” 想象一下，一个温柔的妻子坐在沙发上，也许还有篝火、书籍和音乐。”

达尔文在他的清单下面潦草地写着：“结婚，结婚，结婚QED。” 然而，史蒂文·约翰逊在《有远见的人：我们如何做出最重要的决定》中写道，“我们没有证据表明他实际上是如何权衡这些相互竞争的论点的。” 约翰逊是《我们如何走到现在》和其他流行思想史著作的作者，他不禁注意到达尔文决策过程的平庸。 他指出，本杰明·富兰克林使用了一种更先进的赞成与反对的技术：在富兰克林所谓的“审慎代数”中，为每个列出的项目分配一个数字权重，然后消除平衡的项目。 （“如果我发现一个 Reason pro 等于两个 Reason con，我就会剔除这三个...... 因此，我最终找到了平衡所在，”富兰克林向一位朋友解释道。） 约翰逊写道，即使是这种方法也是草率的并且依赖于直觉。 “做出有远见的选择的技巧——需要长时间深思熟虑的决定，其后果可能持续多年的决定，”他总结道，“奇怪的是，这是一项被低估的技能。”

我们说我们“决定”结婚、生孩子、住在特定的城市或从事特定的职业，从某种意义上来说这是真的。 但我们实际上如何做出这些选择呢？ 生活的悖论之一是，我们的重大决定往往比我们的小决定更不经过深思熟虑。 我们苦恼于在 Netflix 上播放什么内容，然后让电视节目说服我们搬到纽约；购买一台新笔记本电脑可能需要数周的互联网研究，但改变生活的分手背后的深思熟虑可能只需要几瓶酒。 我们并不比古代波斯人先进，希罗多德说，古代波斯人通过两次讨论来做出重大决定：一次是在醉酒时，一次是在清醒时。

约翰逊希望改革我们。 他研究了许多具有深远影响的复杂决策，例如巴拉克·奥巴马总统及其顾问做出的选择，批准对巴基斯坦阿伯塔巴德的乌萨马·本·拉登的据点进行突袭，然后展示了负责人如何利用“决策科学”（行为经济学、心理学和管理学交叉领域的一个研究领域）的见解。 他认为我们应该将这些技巧应用到我们自己的生活中。

我从未需要决定是否对可疑的恐怖分子营地发动秘密突袭，但我已经做出了一些重大决定。 去年夏天，我和妻子生了一个男婴。 他的存在表明，在某个时刻，我决定成为一名父亲。 但我有吗？ 我从来没有练习过任何谨慎代数；我并没有列出利弊清单，并在权衡之后得出结论，生孩子是个好主意，而是逐渐地、无意中从不特别想要孩子转变为想要孩子，从想要孩子转变为和妻子一起生孩子。 如果我做了一个决定，那也不是一个非常决定性的决定。 托尔斯泰在《战争与和平》中写道，虽然一位纸上谈兵的将军可能会想象自己“在地图上分析某些战役”然后发布命令，但真正的将军永远不会发现自己处于“某些事件的开始”；相反，他永远处于一系列事件的中间，每一个事件都是无尽因果链中的一个环节。 “难道是我让拿破仑一直到了莫斯科？” 托尔斯泰笔下的库图佐夫将军感到好奇。 “什么时候决定的？ 是在昨天，当我向普拉托夫发出撤退命令时，还是在前一天晚上，当我打瞌睡并告诉本尼格森下达命令时？ 还是更早一些？” 与拿破仑占领莫斯科不同，我儿子的出生是一个欢乐的时刻。 不过，就像库图佐夫一样，我无法解释它：这是一个重大的选择，但我无法在空间或时间上准确地指出它的形成过程。

对于托尔斯泰来说，重大决策的自行决策倾向是存在的最大谜团之一。 它表明我们讲述的关于我们生活的故事不足以反映其真正的复杂性。 约翰逊打算提供一条摆脱托尔斯泰难题的出路。 他想让我们成为自己故事的作家，而不是读者。 这样做需要解决生活中的基本问题之一：我们对自己的改变方式负责吗？

理想情况下，我们应该无所不知、头脑清醒。 事实上，我们在不完美的条件下做出决定，这阻碍了我们深思熟虑。 约翰逊解释说，这是“有限理性”的问题。 选择受到先前选择的限制；事实未被发现、忽视或误解；决策者会受到集体思维和自己容易犯错的想法的影响。 最复杂的决策都包含着“相互冲​​突的目标”和“未被发现的选择”，要求我们预测未来的可能性，而这些可能性只能在“不同程度的不确定性”下才能把握，但令人困惑。 （婚姻争吵的可能性必须以某种方式与创作科学杰作的可能性进行比较。） 约翰逊说，生活中真正重要的选择“不能用单一的尺度来理解”。 假设你得到了两份工作：一份在健康合作伙伴公司，该公司为世界上最需要帮助的人提供医疗服务，另一份在高盛。 您必须考虑哪种选择在今天、今年晚些时候以及几十年后最有吸引力；这在情感、经济和道德上都更可取；哪个对您、您的家庭和社会都更好。 从这个多维矩阵中，必须做出决定。

约翰逊报告说，专业决策者使用决策流程来应对这种复杂性。 许多最好的流程是分阶段展开的——发散阶段可能先于收敛阶段——并且由小组进行。 （达尔文可能会在分歧阶段将他的朋友分成两个对立的团队，然后在他们之间进行辩论。） 这个决定可能会变成一次迭代的冒险。 在一系列被称为“设计专家研讨会”（这个概念源自产品设计领域）的会议中，一个大问题被分成多个子问题，每个子问题被分配给一个小组；然后，各小组向整个团队展示他们的工作，接收反馈，重新组合和修改，如此循环直至做出决定。 （对于十九世纪巴黎的建筑师来说，参加专家研讨会意味着要修改到最后一刻，甚至是在将设计交付给评审团的路上。） 专家研讨会很有用，不仅因为它们打破了工作，还因为它们迫使具有不同优先级和敏感性的群体（程序员和设计师、建筑师和房地产开发商）进行互动，从而拓宽了可用观点的范围。

在像荷兰皇家壳牌这样的公司中，增长需要投资昂贵的企业，例如港口、油井和管道，决策者使用“情景规划”来想象这些投资可能会如何发挥作用。 （约翰逊写道，情景规划入门工具包包含三种可能的未来：“你构建一种模型，情况会变得更好，一种模型会变得更糟，还有一种模型会变得奇怪。”）军事规划者使用在战场或桌子周围进行的沉浸式战争游戏，以将更多的“决策图”带入视野。 在这样的游戏中，我们的敌人会发现我们无法预见的可能性，从而改善我们个人想象力的匮乏。 由于游戏可以反复玩，决策者可以“倒带”，探索“决策树”的许多分支。

上演一场关于未来婚姻的战争游戏会很奇怪。 尽管如此，约翰逊写道，决策科学对我们个人来说还是有教训的。 在《远见卓识》的后期，他讲述了自己使用决策科学策略说服妻子带着两个孩子从纽约搬到湾区的经历。 约翰逊从直觉开始——红杉很美丽；科技领域很酷，但很快就超越了它们。 他进行了“全方位分析”，得出了关于搬家在经济上、心理上（搬到一个新城市会让他感觉更年轻吗？）和存在意义（他是否想成为“成年后大部分时间都住在一个地方的人”？）的各种结论。 约翰逊在 PowerPoint 中总结了他的发现，然后将其展示给他的妻子，她提出了他没有预见到的反对意见（她所有的朋友都住在布鲁克林）。 最终，他们签订了合同。 他们会搬家，但如果两年后她想返回纽约，他们会这么做，“不问任何问题”——倒带。

七年后，他们对两岸的生活感到满意。 约翰逊会从“举办多学科专家研讨会”来探讨他家人的举动中受益吗？ 可能不会。 尽管如此，他写道，决策科学的原则——“寻求关于选择的不同观点，挑战你的假设，明确地努力绘制变量”——构成了富兰克林和达尔文所制定的赞成和反对清单的“一步”。 回顾自己的决定，约翰逊至少可以确信自己做出了这一决定。

约翰逊的书是悠久传统的一部分。 几个世纪以来，哲学家们一直试图了解我们如何做出决定，以及是什么让任何给定的决定合理或不合理、理性或非理性。 “决策理论”是他们的共同目标，它倾向于认为正确的决策源于价值观。 面对选择——我们应该主修经济学还是艺术史？——我们首先问自己我们看重什么，然后寻求最大化这个价值。

从这个角度来看，决策本质上是一个价值最大化方程。 如果你要出去并且无法决定是否带伞，你可以通过遵循一个公式来做出决定，该公式对下雨的可能性、你在无阻碍地散步时的愉悦感以及你被淋湿时的不快感进行权重分配。 大多数决策都比这更复杂，但决策理论的承诺是，从在阿伯塔巴德发动突袭到在北海挖油井，一切都有一个公式。 输入你的价值观，正确的选择就会出现。

近几十年来，一些哲学家对决策理论越来越不满意。 他们指出，当我们不确定自己关心什么，或者当我们预计自己关心的事情可能会发生变化时，它就变得没那么有用了。 在 2006 年一篇题为《重大决策：选择、转变、漂流》的文章中，已故以色列哲学家埃德娜·乌尔曼-玛格丽特要求我们想象自己是“早期社会主义犹太复国主义先驱”之一，他们在二十世纪之交梦想从欧洲移居巴勒斯坦，成为“他们理想中的新犹太人”。 她观察到，这种变化“改变了一个人的生活计划和内心”；人们可能会说一个先前存在的“老人”，在布达佩斯浏览书店，以及一个后来存在的“新人”，在沙漠中耕种。 此举的目的不是最大化一个人的价值。 而是要重新配置它们，重写人们目前生活的方程式。

乌尔曼-玛格丽特怀疑这种变革性的选择是否可以被评价为合理或不合理、理性或非理性。 她讲述了一个男人的故事，他“犹豫要不要孩子，因为他不想成为父母那样的‘无聊类型’”。 “最后，他确实决定要一个孩子，随着时间的推移，他确实采用了他父母朋友的无聊特征——但他很高兴！” 谁的价值被最大化——旧人的还是新人的？ 因为没有价值最大化公式可以捕捉到这样的选择，乌尔曼-玛格丽特建议，我们不要将这个男人描述为“决定”生孩子，而是说他“选择”生孩子——“选择”（用她的话说）是我们改变价值观而不是最大化价值观时所做的事情。

她认为，“选择情境”的本质解释了为什么人们“实际上在处理重大决定时比处理普通决定时更加随意和随意”。 然而，困扰我们的是我们尚未探索的选择。 购买斯巴鲁的决策者不会关注丰田可能的情况：丰田并不代表她自己具有不同价值观的版本。 然而，选择者会沉思“一个人没有结婚的人，一个没有移民到的国家，一个没有追求的职业”，在被拒绝的选择所暗示的“影子存在”中看到她可以用来评估她现实生活的“价值、成功或意义”的“标准”。

人们可能希望进行一些研究可以弥合旧人和新人之间的鸿沟。 在 2013 年发表的一篇题​​为“当你怀孕时你不能期待什么”的论文中，L. 一个。 耶鲁大学哲学家保罗写道：“也许你认为你可以知道拥有一个孩子是什么感觉，即使你从未有过孩子，因为你可以读到或听到别人的见证。 您错了。” 保罗引用了哲学家大卫·刘易斯的观点，他提出了所谓的 Vegemite 原则：如果你从未尝过 Vegemite，这是一种由啤酒酵母制成的神秘而受人喜爱的澳大利亚“食品涂抹酱”，那么无论是对其外观的描述（黑色、粘稠、植物味）还是其他涂抹酱（花生酱、果酱、花生酱）的体验都不足以告诉你是否喜欢它。 同样，保罗认为，“与别人的孩子在一起并不足以了解你自己的情况会是什么样子。” 她解释说：

照顾其他孩子，拥有侄女和侄子或更小的兄弟姐妹——所有这些都可能是美妙的（或可怕的）经历，但它们与拥有自己的孩子在性质上有所不同，也许大致类似于原创艺术品具有审美价值的方式，部分原因在于其起源。 。 。 。 与别人的孩子相处的经历可能会让你了解抱婴儿、换尿布或拿着奶瓶是什么感觉，但不会教你创造、携带、出生和抚养自己的孩子是什么感觉。

在生孩子之前，您可能喜欢泡吧、跳伞和迷幻药；你可能会在事业、旅行、烹饪或综合健身中找到满足感；你可能只是享受做你想做的事的自由。 生孩子会让你失去这些快乐。 然而，作为父母，您可能不会想念他们。 事实上，你可能更喜欢换尿布、争论连体衣和看《冰雪奇缘》。 这些活动对于没有孩子的你来说可能听起来像是一种折磨，但为人父母的你可能会发现它们被爱所照亮，并因此得到救赎。 你可能最终会成为一个不同的人——父母。 问题是你无法提前真正知道“为人父母”是什么样的。 对于保罗来说，这种困境令人兴奋。 为什么今天的价值观决定明天的价值观？ 在她 2014 年出版的《变革性体验》一书中，她提出，“真实”的生活需要偶尔将旧的自我抛在身后，“创造和发现新的自我”。 活着的一部分就是等待“你将成为谁”的“启示”。

在我们儿子出生前的几个月里，我们越来越感到自己的无知。 “我们不知道自己在等什么，”我的妻子说。 我们事先就知道他什么时候出生——超声波检查显示他异常大，并安排了剖腹产——但他出生的那天早上却以一种奇怪的熟悉感展开。 我喝了咖啡，烤了一个英式松饼，然后读了新闻；我把去医院的衣服装进每天上班带的包里。 十一点，我和妻子上了车。 她的母亲和一位家庭朋友开车送我们去。 在正门，我们与他们拥抱告别。

“祝你好运！” 我婆婆说。 “你的生活即将永远改变！”

“谢谢，”我说。 “你们要去哪里？”

“好市多，”她说。

我们走进去。 在楼上一个用窗帘隔开的角落里，我妻子躺在医院的病床上。 在大约一个小时的时间里，我们与护士闲聊，他们猜测了婴儿的体重，还与外科医生（碰巧是我们的大学同学）闲聊。 （“Heyyyyy！”她到达时说道。） 有时候，我们只能独自一人。 我们手牵手，互相看着对方。

最终，一名助手帮助我的妻子坐上轮椅。 在两名穿着超大手术服的护士的陪伴下，我推着她沿着一条长长的走廊走向手术室。 在里面，医生们正在听收音机里的《天国的阶梯》。 在这一切之中，我很欣赏吉米·佩奇的吉他独奏。 之后，我抱着我们的孩子坐在同一个走廊里。 我曾想知道，第一次见到他时，我是否会感到改变。 我感觉就像以前的我一样。 然而，我所知道的单词没有一个与我的经历相符。 我用手感觉到他的呼吸。 他安静而平静，温暖而清醒，用深蓝色的眼睛看着我——一个真正的新人。

芝加哥大学哲学家艾格尼丝·卡拉德 (Agnes Callard) 对突然转变的想法持怀疑态度。 她还坚信，无论看起来或感觉如何，我们选择如何改变。 在她动人而又深刻的著作《渴望：成为的力量》中，她写道，“成为父母既不是偶然发生在你​​身上的事情，也不是你决定发生在你身上的事情。” 相反，卡拉德坚持认为，我们“渴望”通过尝试我们希望有一天拥有的价值观来实现自我转变，就像我们在约会前对着镜子摆一个姿势一样。 对于乌尔曼-玛格丽特文章中那个害怕成为一个无聊父亲的人，卡拉德写道：“当他说‘让我们努力吧’时，他正在积极尝试欣赏为人父母的独特价值观。” 卡拉德看到的不是一瞬间的决定，而是一个更加渐进的过程：“旧人渴望成为新人。”

假设你报名参加了一个古典音乐欣赏班，你的第一个作业是听一首交响乐。 你戴上耳机，按下播放键，然后就睡着了。 问题是你实际上并不想听古典音乐；你想听古典音乐。你只是想要。 卡拉德认为，有抱负是一种常见的人类活动：有抱负的葡萄酒爱好者、艺术鉴赏家、体育迷、时尚达人、DJ、高管、登山运动员、行善者、父母和宗教信徒，都在酝酿重视新事物的计划。 此外，许多普通的决定——比如在高盛和健康合作伙伴之间进行选择——也涉及到我们渴望成为谁的问题。

卡拉德区分了愿望和野心。 参加音乐欣赏班的人有的雄心勃勃，有的人志向远大。他们报名并不是因为他们渴望热爱古典音乐，而是因为这门课很简单。 从第一天起，他们就知道自己看重什么：成绩。 （“将雄心壮志转化为抱负是任何教师的工作职责之一，”卡拉德指出。） 这些雄心勃勃的学生发现很容易解释他们为什么要上这门课。 但有抱负的人必须适应一定数量的尴尬假装。 如果有人问你为什么入学，如果你说你被古典音乐的深邃之美所感动，那你就太过分了。 更难沟通的事实是，你对其价值有一些模糊的感觉，你希望未来的自己能够正确地理解它。

在有志者能够充分解释他们的动机之前，他们常常低估他们的目标。 一位有抱负的画家会说她发现绘画令人放松，而不是试图解释她希望通过艺术表达什么。 卡拉德总结道，一个抱负有两副面孔：一张近的面孔，代表它“比实际情况更小”；一张远的面孔，有抱负者不愿意描述，因为它“使她当前的活动超出了其应有的地位”。

做一个善意的骗子是我们自我转变的关键。 “想一想，当一个好学生感觉自己打瞌睡时，是什么样的想法促使她强迫自己听交响乐，”卡拉德写道：

她提醒自己，她的成绩和老师对她的看法取决于她将写的关于这篇文章的文章；或者她答应自己读完后会得到一份巧克力；或者她在图书馆的玻璃墙听音室里，意识到其他学生的目光在她身上；或者也许她会想象出她未来的音乐自我的浪漫化形象，比如在下雪的夜晚进入音乐厅温暖的灯光。

卡拉德说，这些都是听古典音乐的“坏”理由，但“‘坏’理由是她如何推动自己前进，同时始终将它们视为坏事，也就是说，将它们视为‘真正’原因的占位符。”

当我们有抱负时，不善表达并不意味着不合理或无能力。 事实上，事实可能恰恰相反。 “每个人上大学都是为了‘接受教育’，”卡拉德观察到，“但在我接受教育之前，我并不真正知道教育是什么或为什么它很重要。” 如果我们不能渴望实现我们难以描述的改变，我们就会被困在我们已有的想法中。 我们无法解释自己的原因，这衡量了我们希望走多远。 卡拉德写道，只有当有志者到达目的地后，“她才会说，‘这就是原因。’”

由于愿望需要很长时间才能实现，因此它们总是面临中断的风险。 乌尔曼-玛格丽特 2006 年的论文提到有人选择“离开企业界成为一名艺术家”。 卡拉德将这种举动视为一种愿望的结果——这个过程从小事开始，也许是在艺术博物馆里随意漫步，几年后，当一个人开设了一家陶艺工作室时，这一过程达到了顶峰。 问题在于某些价值观会排斥其他价值观。 一位有抱负的艺术家必须拒绝他曾经渴望的企业美德，并拥抱创造性的美德。 如果家庭疾病迫使他放弃艺术计划，他最终可能会随波逐流——对企业生活不再抱有幻想，但却无法抓住艺术存在的真正满足感。 卡拉德写道，立志就是以尚不存在的未来自我的标准来评判现在的自我。 但这可能会让我们像吊兰一样在空中扎根，希望得到可能永远不会到达的土壤。

卡拉德重温了保罗的《当你在期待时你无法期待什么》。 在那篇论文中，保罗探讨了维吉麦原则的一个奇怪的结果：如果没有理性的方式来决定要一个孩子——因为你不知道自己从未经历过什么——那么也没有合理的理由对没有孩子感到失望。 （保罗指出，这种失望并不是“错误的，或应受谴责的，或主观上不合理的”，而是非理性的。） 卡拉德不同意。 她将不孕视为一种渴望中断的形式。 她写道，一位有抱负却不能生孩子的母亲感到悲伤是理性的，“即使——事实上，部分原因是——她不太明白自己会失去什么，情况也是如此。”

在我们有了儿子之前，我开始探索作为父母的“近面”。 我注意到婴儿和儿童是多么可爱，并把我们的空房间想象成托儿所；我设想我和妻子带着孩子去我们家附近的海滩（我的版本是“在下雪的夜晚进入音乐厅温暖的灯光”）。 我知道这些想象并不是关于生孩子的真实事实——显然，生孩子不仅仅是可爱。 尽管如此，我还是无法抓住父亲“遥远的面孔”。 这是我渴望知道的事情。

事实证明，我和妻子在生孩子​​方面遇到了困难。 我们花了五年时间才走出不孕不育的迷宫。 在那段时间的大部分时间里，我们都生活在卡拉德所描述的“一种独特的悲伤之中，这种悲伤适合失去你刚刚开始尝试了解的东西。” 卡拉德指出，这种悲伤与人们在“不得不放弃成为母亲的教育愿望”后可能感到的失望相辅相成：“那些必须放弃养育孩子的梦想的有抱负的大学生很容易觉得她依靠大学经历来让自己的生活变得有意义。” 卡拉德引用了历史学家伊莱恩·泰勒·梅所著的一本关于不孕症的书《应许之地的贫瘠之地》。 “悲伤——失去，”一位女士告诉梅。 “我花了六年的时间试图成为一名母亲，但这超出了我的控制范围。 一时间我无法向前看。 我想，如果我不这样做，我该如何定义自己呢？ 如果不是父母我又是什么？” 如果我们最大的转变是瞬间发生的，事情可能会更容易，因为那样我们就不需要生活在渴望的状态中。 确定我们是谁，我们永远不会陷入自我之中。

去年春天，在我儿子出生之前，我读了《愿望》，我经常和我的妻子谈论它。 卡拉德的论点尤其令我们震惊，他认为为人父母本质上是一种渴望。 父母期待与特定的人建立爱的关系。 然而，这个人并没有完全成形；他还没有完全成型。他的独特性历经了许多年才得以显现。 出于这个原因，成为一个“雄心勃勃的父母”——一个提前计划他会爱孩子什么的人——是没有意义的。 卡拉德总结道，最好“出于最不成熟的原因而成为父母”，因为这“让我们的孩子能够了解为人父母对我们意味着什么”；反过来，父母的爱必须“能够将自己塑造成人格，而人格本身就会形成确定的形状”。

在很大程度上，卡拉德的书是一个系统的概述，处于当下之外。 尽管如此，她写道，对于有抱负的人来说，“同时发生的事情也是生活。” 现在我们的儿子在这里，我们完全生活在这同时。 我们不希望现在或其神秘结束。 每一天都令人着迷且意义无穷。 最近，我看着父亲的脸，就像他看着我儿子的脸一样。 后来，我们听到我儿子学会了一种新的笑声。 每次他看着我们，他都会以他自己的方式看待我们。 就像自动翻页的书页一样，有意义的时刻很快就会到来。 很难将它们视为通往其他地方的踏脚石。 ❖
